analysis.one_liner: Requires cosmetics makers to register with the FDA, report serious injuries, and lets the FDA order recalls.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan sponsorship from Sens. Feinstein (D-CA) and Collins (R-ME) and 3 cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote and expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have, for the first time, required cosmetics manufacturers to register their facilities with the FDA, list their ingredients, and report serious injuries linked to their products. It would have let the FDA order mandatory recalls of dangerous cosmetics, review at least five cosmetic ingredients for safety each year, set manufacturing standards, require disclosure of fragrance allergens on labels, and begin a rule to ban PFAS 'forever chemicals' in cosmetics. Companies with over $10 million in annual cosmetics sales would pay registration fees to fund the oversight; small makers below $500,000 in sales would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly everyone who uses makeup, shampoo, lotion, and hair dye. Today the FDA has almost no power over cosmetics: it cannot order a recall, does not know which facilities make what, and companies do not have to report when a product hospitalizes someone. This bill would have changed that, and would have specifically protected people with fragrance allergies, children, and pregnant women through labeling rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who uses cosmetics and personal care products

how_it_helps.text: Gives the FDA mandatory recall authority over cosmetics found likely to cause serious health consequences or death, plus the power to suspend a facility's registration so its products cannot be sold [S2][S3].

Requires companies to report serious adverse events — deaths, hospitalizations, disfigurement, hair loss — to the FDA within 15 business days, and to file annual reports of all adverse events [S2][S3].
Requires annual FDA safety reviews of at least five cosmetic ingredients, with public comment, and lets the FDA set limits, require warnings, or declare an ingredient not safe [S2][S3].

Requires labels to disclose 26 named fragrance allergens above set concentrations and, for internet sales, display the same warnings online as on packaging; consumers could contact manufacturers to ask about unlisted ingredients [S3].
Directs the FDA to propose a rule banning intentionally added PFAS in cosmetics, a class of persistent chemicals linked to health concerns [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large cosmetics manufacturers and their suppliers. Companies with more than $10 million in annual cosmetics sales would pay FDA registration fees, and all registered manufacturers would bear the cost of facility registration, ingredient statements, adverse-event tracking, recordkeeping, and eventual good-manufacturing-practice compliance. Fragrance and flavor suppliers would have to turn over complete ingredient lists to the FDA on request. Companies under $500,000 in sales are exempt entirely, and those under $2 million face lighter requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large cosmetics makers and fragrance suppliers

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state rules: once the FDA selects an ingredient for review, states cannot set new requirements on it for over a year, and states cannot add rules on registration, recalls, or adverse-event reporting at all. That would cap protections at the federal level, which historically moves slower than states like California [S3].
At five ingredients reviewed per year, a safety pass through the thousands of chemicals used in cosmetics would take decades, leaving most ingredients unreviewed for a generation [S2][S3].

FDA cosmetics oversight would be funded by registration fees paid by the largest companies, and the FDA must pick the annual ingredient-review list 'in consultation with the cosmetic industry' — a structure that ties the regulator's budget and agenda to the regulated industry [S3].

Compliance costs — registration, ingredient filings, recordkeeping retained for years — fall on manufacturers, and while small businesses are exempted, firms between the exemption thresholds face real paperwork burdens that could nudge marginal small brands out [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real and address a genuine gap: cosmetics are one of the least-regulated product categories Americans put on their bodies daily, and the FDA currently lacks even recall power. The main concessions to industry — partial preemption of state law, a slow five-ingredients-a-year review pace, and industry consultation over the review agenda — weaken the bill but do not erase its value. The fee-funded oversight model is a tradeoff: it avoids taxpayer cost but embeds industry in the regulator's financing.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee never took the bill up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Dianne Feinstein introduced the Personal Care Products Safety Act on June 17, 2021, together with Sen. Susan Collins, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S3][S5].
That referral was the bill's last recorded action: no committee vote, no markup, and no Senate floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended [S1][S5].

The bill would have required cosmetics facility registration with fees for large companies, annual FDA review of at least five ingredients, mandatory recall authority, serious adverse event reporting, fragrance allergen labeling, and a proposed PFAS ban [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large cosmetics manufacturers are better off: they never had to register facilities with the FDA, pay registration fees, report hospitalizations and deaths tied to their products, submit to records inspections, or face mandatory recalls — the status quo of minimal federal oversight continued. Consumers gained nothing from the bill's death; the safety gap it addressed remains.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat and a Republican together, and its three cosponsors split 2 Democrats and 1 Republican; no recorded opposition ever materialized because the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: Companies over $10 million in cosmetics sales would pay registration fees and all registered makers would face facility registration, ingredient statements, adverse-event reporting, records inspection, and mandatory recall authority. The industry's interest in avoiding these requirements runs directly against the bill's consumer safety purpose.

Suppliers would have to give the FDA the complete ingredient lists of their fragrance and flavor formulas on request within 30 days, ending the trade secrecy that currently shields the 'fragrance' line on product labels. Consumers with allergies would gain the disclosure.

Manufacturers under $500,000 in sales are exempt entirely, and those between $500,000 and $2 million face lighter registration and reporting requirements. They escape the compliance costs larger firms would bear, though they stay outside the safety net the bill builds for consumers.
